fatal_errors: The proposed intervention omits the target high-energy ball milling and spark-plasma-sintering treatment entirely.

The mechanism reverses the target interpretation: it claims Ti-induced lattice distortion facilitates glide and softens the alloy, whereas the target attributes strengthening to nanocrystalline grain boundaries, milling-induced dislocation density, solid-solution effects, and an FCC/BCC phase mixture.
The assumed single-phase state is incompatible with the target mixed 83% FCC and 17% BCC nanocrystalline structure.

The Ti-free CoCrFeNi baseline does not isolate deformation mechanism cleanly because removing Ti changes composition, phase stability, stacking-fault energy, lattice parameter, and potentially grain structure simultaneously.
No cited evidence supports the counterintuitive assertion that greater Ti-induced lattice distortion lowers dislocation barriers rather than impeding glide.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses low strength through dislocation behavior and supplies explicit boundaries and a nominal falsification rule, but it does not reconstruct the processing route, structural mediator, baseline, or measured outcome of the target. Its comparison could test whether Ti-containing and Ti-free alloys deform differently, yet it cannot uniquely attribute the difference to local lattice distortion without independently matching phase constitution, grain size, defect density, and texture. In-situ TEM also risks thin-foil and free-surface artifacts, so bulk slip and pile-up behavior would require complementary diffraction, microscopy, and mechanical measurements. Most importantly, the predicted softening conflicts with the target result of approximately 675 Hv hardness and 1894 MPa compressive strength after milling and SPS, where grain refinement, accumulated defects, densification, and the FCC/BCC mixture govern strengthening.
